## TL;DR

Completed a cross-theme QA pass for the main RepoOS pages. The rendered contrast
audit passed its complete configured matrix, and a headless Playwright pass
found no horizontal overflow or page errors on Work, Releases, Settings, Agents
or Checks at 375px and 1280px across eight themes in light and dark modes. No
reproducible product defect was found, so there was no code change or regression
test to add. The observed scope and its limits are recorded in
`docs/qa/2026-11-themes.md`.

## Work and rationale

I began with the task file and the repository's rendered contrast audit notes.
The task is specifically concerned with light and alternative themes, so I
used both the existing rendered audit and a viewport pass. The audit is valuable
because it measures rendered text against composited backgrounds rather than
merely checking token definitions. Its existing scope covers 16 theme scopes
and 14 UI states, including task drawers and Settings.

The first UI-only build passed. The contrast command initially could not run
because it imports the compiled CLI module from `dist`; after a full build it
ran successfully. This was a build-order requirement, not a product failure.
The final run examined 15,252 visible text runs and found no text below its
WCAG floor. It classified 320 runs under existing central exemptions, 64
for disabled components, and 14 gradient-clipped logo runs as expected.

I then started the auth-less dev server from this task worktree and used only
headless Playwright. The pass visited `/work`, `/releases`, `/settings`,
`/agents`, and `/checks` at 375px and 1280px. It applied each of the eight
configured theme families and both modes, then checked document/body widths
against the viewport and collected page errors. No overflow or page errors
were observed in the 160 route/theme/mode/viewport combinations. No visible
browser or user Chrome was opened.

I wrote the evidence and coverage note to `docs/qa/2026-11-themes.md`. It
explicitly distinguishes the rendered contrast audit's configured coverage
from the added route/layout pass: the audit tests drawers and Settings but does
not include Releases/deployment screens. The Playwright pass establishes
stability and viewport fit for Releases, but not a text-by-text contrast verdict
there. I did not widen the contrast audit or alter exemptions because this
pass did not reproduce a failure and the acceptance task did not authorize
changing the audit matrix.

## Approaches tried

- Ran `bun run build:ui` to confirm UI compilation. It passed.
- Ran the rendered audit before a full build. It correctly reported that
  `dist/commands/ui-contrast-audit.js` was unavailable. This established that
  the CLI build was needed before the audit could execute.
- Ran `bun run build`, then `bun run contrast:audit`. The configured full
  matrix passed.
- Used headless Playwright against the auth-less server for route and viewport
  checks across all configured themes and modes. The pass reported zero
  overflow cases and zero uncaught page errors.

## Challenges and blockers

The main practical issue was the contrast audit's dependency on compiled
artifacts after a UI-only build. A full build resolved this without source
changes. The existing rendered audit's documented screen coverage omits
Releases and deployment pages. I captured that limitation in the QA note rather
than treating the route/layout pass as proof of contrast or expanding a
separate audit scope without a reproduced defect.

No human-only verification was needed. All browser checks were headless and
used the auth-less development server.

## Key learnings

The repository already has a strong rendered contrast gate across the declared
theme scopes and drawer states; the extra QA value here came from exercising
Releases and checking narrow viewport fit across all named themes. The tests
answered different questions: rendered contrast measured text legibility in
covered states, while the route pass checked app stability and horizontal
fit. Keeping that distinction in the report avoids overstating what was
verified. Since neither pass showed a defect, adding a speculative CSS change
or a test tied to an invented failure would have reduced confidence rather
than improved it.
